questions.title: Left vs. right multiplication in OFT: are the dimensions consistent?
questions.question_body: In Section 3, the paper says OFT optimizes an orthogonal matrix \(\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) for a pretrained linear layer \(\mathbf{W}^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}\), and modifies the forward pass from \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x}\) to \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{R} \mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x}\). I am confused about the shapes: if \(\mathbf{W}^0\) is \(d \times n\), then \((\mathbf{W}^0)^\top\) is \(n \times d\), which multiplies \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) to produce \(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^n\). After left-multiplying \(\mathbf{R}\), \(\mathbf{R} \mathbf{W}^0\) is still \(d \times n\), so the shapes work out. But what is the practical interpretation of left-multiplying by \(\mathbf{R}\) versus the more common convention \(\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}\)? Could the authors clarify the dimensional conventions they use across MLPs, attention projections, and embeddings, and ensure there is no mismatch for convolutional layers?

questions.title: What exactly does “preserving pairwise angles between neurons” mean in OFT?
questions.question_body: The motivation for OFT is to preserve the pairwise angles between neurons by applying the same orthogonal transform \(\mathbf{R}\) to all columns of \(\mathbf{W}^0\). If each neuron is a column vector \(\mathbf{w}^0_i\), then after OFT we have \(\mathbf{w}'_i = \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{w}^0_i\). Because \(\mathbf{R}\) is orthogonal, \(\langle \mathbf{w}'_i, \mathbf{w}'_j \rangle = \langle \mathbf{w}^0_i, \mathbf{w}^0_j \rangle\). My confusion is: in practical networks with nonlinearities (e.g., GELU), layer norms, and residuals, how does preserving these angles translate to better downstream generalization? Is there any empirical or theoretical link showing that maintaining these intra-layer geometric relationships correlates with task performance?

questions.title: Cayley transform details: does it cover all orthogonal matrices and is it numerically stable?
questions.question_body: The paper uses the Cayley parameterization \(\mathbf{R} = (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf{Q}=-\mathbf{Q}^\top\). I recall that the Cayley transform maps skew-symmetric matrices to orthogonal matrices with no eigenvalue equal to \(-1\), and typically yields \(\det(\mathbf{R})=+1\). 1) Does this parameterization exclude some orthogonal matrices (those with eigenvalue \(-1\)) and is that a practical limitation? 2) How is the inverse \((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) computed stably in mixed precision? 3) Would using the matrix exponential \(\exp(\mathbf{Q})\) be more principled on the Stiefel/orthogonal manifold, and what trade-offs led you to choose Cayley over \(\exp\)?

questions.title: How does the parameter count \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1) d m\) for BOFT(m, b) derive?
questions.question_body: Section 4 states that BOFT(\(m, b\)) takes \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1) d m\) effective trainable parameters for finetuning a linear layer of size \(d \times n\). Could the authors derive this formula explicitly? In particular: 1) How many independent parameters are there in each \(2b \times 2b\) orthogonal block (after accounting for orthogonality constraints)? 2) How many such blocks exist per butterfly component at dimension \(d\)? 3) How does this scale across the \(m\) stacked components? A step-by-step counting argument would help.

questions.title: Why does BOFT(\(\log\frac{2d}{b}, b\)) guarantee a dense \(\mathbf{R}\)?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that BOFT\((\log \tfrac{2d}{b}, b)\) yields a dense orthogonal \(\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\). Can you provide a formal argument that, with this number of butterfly components and block size, the induced information-transmission graph connects every input index to every output index (i.e., no structural zeros remain)? A small worked example for \(d=16\) and several \(b\) choices would be great.

questions.title: Handling non-power-of-two dimensions and mixed radix in the butterfly factorization
questions.question_body: The recursive definition of the butterfly matrices assumes \(d = 2^N\). Many layers in practice have dimensions not equal to a power of two (e.g., \(d=768\) or \(d=4096\)). How does BOFT handle such cases? Do you (a) pad to the next power of two and mask, (b) use mixed-radix butterfly constructions, or (c) fall back to a hybrid structure? What are the parameter and compute implications of the chosen approach?

questions.title: What are “free edges” in the information transmission framework?
questions.question_body: In Section 3, the paper introduces an information-transmission view and mentions the desideratum of “minimum free edges,” with the note that some edges are not trainable due to orthogonality (e.g., in a \(d \times d\) orthogonal matrix with \(d\) non-zeros, those entries must be \(\pm 1\)). I am confused about the precise definition of “free edges.” Are these the degrees of freedom after enforcing orthogonality constraints, or literally the non-zero positions that remain tunable? Could you formalize this notion and show how it leads to \(\mathcal{O}(d \log d)\) parameters for butterfly vs. \(\mathcal{O}(d^2)\) for dense?

questions.title: Does dense connectivity in the graph always imply a dense final matrix product?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that ensuring every source node reaches every sink node in the unrolled graph implies the product \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{B}_m \cdots \mathbf{B}_1\) is dense. Is it possible for specific parameter values (e.g., cancellations across factors) to create exact zeros, even when the connectivity graph is dense? If so, is the claim probabilistic (“almost surely dense” under random continuous parameters), or is there a structural argument that prevents cancellations?

questions.title: Why is the block-diagonal OFT unable to approximate classic transforms like DFT?
questions.question_body: The paper states that the block-diagonal orthogonal parameterization in OFT cannot recover classic linear transforms such as the discrete Fourier transform, whereas butterfly-based BOFT can. Could you provide a proof sketch or intuition for why a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix (with fixed block partition by index) cannot represent the DFT matrix (up to permutations), while a butterfly composition can?

questions.title: Orthogonality of butterfly components built from \(2 \times 2\) blocks
questions.question_body: The construction claims that all butterfly components \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(d, k)\) can be made orthogonal because their non-zero pattern is a permutation of \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(d, 2)\), and \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(d, 2)\) can be parameterized as a block-diagonal matrix of \(2 \times 2\) orthogonals (via Cayley or Givens). Could you formalize this permutation argument? Specifically, how do we guarantee that permuting rows/columns of an orthogonal block-diagonal matrix yields an orthogonal matrix with the same butterfly sparsity pattern?

questions.title: BOFT identity initialization and gradient flow at \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}\)
questions.question_body: BOFT initializes each butterfly component to identity (equivalently \(\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{0}\) in Cayley). In this case, \(\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{I}\) and the model initially matches the pretrained network. Is there any risk of poor gradient flow or symmetry that makes some parameters locally unidentifiable at initialization? For instance, are there directions in \(\mathbf{Q}\) that produce second-order small changes to the loss, slowing early optimization? Any empirical signs of cold starts when stacking many butterfly components (large \(m\))?

questions.title: How does multiplicative Dropout preserve orthogonality and what is dropped?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes a multiplicative Dropout that randomly chooses a fraction of butterfly components and a fraction of their diagonal blocks and replaces them with identity during training. 1) Does this preserve overall orthogonality at each forward pass? 2) Are the dropped blocks’ parameters updated via gradients (i.e., are they bypassed but still receive gradients), or are their gradients zero? 3) How are \(p_1\) and \(p_2\) chosen to avoid breaking dense connectivity and to avoid under-parameterizing the effective transform?

questions.title: Expressivity theorem: how many butterfly factors are needed to span \(O(d)\)?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 states that BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size and suggests that products of butterfly matrices and their transposes can approximate all \(d \times d\) orthogonal matrices (a kaleidoscope hierarchy). Could the authors provide a precise statement with complexity: how many butterfly factors (and of what sizes) are sufficient for universal approximation of \(O(d)\)? Is \(l=d-1\) in the product \(\mathbf{B}_{d-1,1}\mathbf{B}^\top_{d-1,2} \cdots \mathbf{B}_{1,1}\mathbf{B}^\top_{1,2}\) necessary or just sufficient? Any known lower bounds?

questions.title: Runtime and memory overhead: how does BOFT compare to OFT and LoRA?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that BOFT incurs additional runtime overhead because it multiplies multiple sparse (but structured) orthogonal factors each iteration. Could you quantify the training-time FLOPs and memory overhead relative to: (a) full OFT with a single dense \(\mathbf{R}\), and (b) LoRA with rank \(r\)? For a layer of size \(d \times n\), what is the complexity per forward/backward pass when using BOFT(\(m, b\))? Any practical guidance on choosing \(m, b\) under a fixed wall-clock budget?

questions.title: Does left-multiplying by \(\mathbf{R}\) change the function class when \(\mathbf{W}^0\) is followed by nonlinearity?
questions.question_body: Consider a layer output \(\mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0)^\top \mathbf{x}\) followed by a pointwise nonlinearity \(\sigma\). Since \(\mathbf{R}\) changes the basis in the input subspace of the pretrained weight \(\mathbf{W}^0\), is there any invariance if \(\sigma\) is linear (obviously yes) versus when \(\sigma\) is nonlinear (ReLU/GELU)? Can \(\mathbf{R}\) be absorbed by later layers in some architectures (e.g., due to LayerNorm)? I want to understand whether \(\mathbf{R}\) meaningfully changes representational capacity in the presence of common architectural elements.

questions.title: How are bias terms and LayerNorm parameters handled under BOFT?
questions.question_body: The paper focuses on transforming weight matrices via left-multiplication with an orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\). What about biases in linear layers and the scaling/shift parameters in LayerNorm? Are they left untouched, or is there a recommended way to combine BOFT with small extra adapters for these affine terms to avoid misalignment after rotation?

questions.title: Applying BOFT to convolutional layers: which dimension is \(d\)?
questions.question_body: For Conv2D layers, weights are typically \((\text{out\_channels}, \text{in\_channels}, k_h, k_w)\). If we flatten to \(d \times n\), which dimension is chosen as \(d\) for the orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\)? Do you rotate input channels (i.e., act on \(\text{in\_channels}\)) or output channels, or both? Any empirical guidance on which choice works best for vision backbones?

questions.title: Numerical orthogonality under mixed precision: do we need re-orthogonalization?
questions.question_body: In practice, training often uses mixed precision and fused kernels. Even with the Cayley transform, finite precision may introduce small deviations from perfect orthogonality. Do you observe any drift in \(\mathbf{R}^\top\mathbf{R}\) over training? Is any periodic re-orthogonalization or projection needed to maintain stability, or is the Cayley parameterization sufficient in FP16/BF16?

questions.title: Why does preserving the spectral norm help stability compared to LoRA?
questions.question_body: You argue that both OFT and BOFT preserve the spectral norm of \(\mathbf{W}^0\) because they left-multiply by an orthogonal matrix, while LoRA perturbs \(\mathbf{W}^0\) additively and may change the spectral norm. Can you provide an intuitive explanation or small example showing how maintaining the top singular value prevents gradient explosion or improves generalization? Are there cases where LoRA can also maintain spectral norms (e.g., with spectral regularization) and close the gap?

questions.title: Hyperparameter selection: how to choose \(m\) and \(b\) under a fixed parameter budget?
questions.question_body: Figure 2 suggests that smaller \(b\) and larger \(m\) can be more parameter-efficient for approximating random orthogonals. In practice, for a given parameter budget P, how should we choose \(m\) and \(b\)? Is there a simple heuristic (e.g., prioritize increasing \(m\) until latency becomes an issue, then increase \(b\))? Any layer-wise adaptation rules for transformers (e.g., larger \(m\) in attention projections vs. MLPs)?

questions.title: Connectivity guarantees under multiplicative Dropout: can BOFT become effectively block-diagonal?
questions.question_body: If multiplicative Dropout replaces some butterfly components or their blocks by identities at random during training, could this create training steps where the effective \(\mathbf{R}\) loses dense connectivity (e.g., degenerates toward block-diagonal), potentially harming gradient signals? Do you enforce any constraints on \(p_1, p_2\) to ensure that, with high probability, the effective transform remains sufficiently connected each iteration?

questions.title: BOFT as learning a bilinear similarity: what is the implied metric?
questions.question_body: Section 5 mentions that BOFT learns a bilinear similarity \(\mathbf{w}^0_i \mathbf{R} \mathbf{x}\) with a strong regularity (orthogonality). Since \(\mathbf{R}\) is orthogonal, the induced bilinear form is not a Mahalanobis metric (which requires positive semidefinite). How should we interpret this bilinear similarity geometrically? Is there a connection to rotating the input space so that fixed neurons \(\mathbf{w}^0_i\) become better aligned with task-relevant directions?

questions.title: Relation to Householder or Givens factorizations: why butterfly?
questions.question_body: Any orthogonal matrix can be decomposed into a product of Householder reflectors or Givens rotations. BOFT instead uses a structured product (butterfly) of sparse orthogonals. Could you compare parameter counts and computational properties between: (a) a product of \(\mathcal{O}(d)\) Householder reflectors, (b) a sparse network of Givens rotations, and (c) your butterfly factors? What makes butterfly particularly attractive for PEFT beyond its DFT heritage?

questions.title: “Smoother interpolation” claim: in what sense is BOFT between identity and full \(O(d)\)?
questions.question_body: The paper says BOFT provides a smoother interpolation between identity (regularity) and the full orthogonal group (expressivity) compared to block-diagonal OFT. Can you formalize this notion of interpolation? For instance, does increasing \(m\) monotonically enlarge the reachable set of \(\mathbf{R}\) (for fixed \(b\))? Is there a measure (e.g., VC dimension or covering number) indicating that BOFT’s hypothesis class grows more gradually or more “uniformly” than block-diagonal’s?

questions.title: Are BOFT transforms shared across layers or per-layer?
questions.question_body: The paper contrasts BOFT with methods that reparameterize each layer’s weights directly and mentions “layer-shared weight matrices.” My reading of OFT/BOFT is that the same \(\mathbf{R}\) is shared across all neurons in a given layer, but not across different layers. Is that correct? Have you tried sharing a single \(\mathbf{R}\) across multiple layers (e.g., all attention projection layers) to further reduce parameters, and what was the effect on performance?

questions.title: Merging multiple finetunings: do BOFT adapters compose nicely?
questions.question_body: If we finetune the same base model on two tasks with BOFT, we obtain two orthogonal matrices \(\mathbf{R}_A\) and \(\mathbf{R}_B\). Is there a principled way to combine them without retraining (e.g., via averaging in the tangent space, composing \(\mathbf{R}_B \mathbf{R}_A\), or using a Procrustes alignment)? Does the butterfly structure help with such composition, or do we lose the sparsity pattern upon merging?

questions.title: On determinant and eigenvalue constraints of Cayley-parameterized \(\mathbf{R}\)
questions.question_body: Since the Cayley transform cannot produce orthogonal matrices with eigenvalue \(-1\), is \(\det(\mathbf{R})\) always \(+1\)? If so, BOFT is constrained to \(SO(d)\), the special orthogonal group. Is excluding \(\det=-1\) transformations ever beneficial (e.g., regularization), or could it limit expressivity in tasks where a reflection is useful? Would augmenting with an occasional Householder reflection fix this if needed?

questions.title: Does BOFT change the effective Lipschitz constant of the network?
questions.question_body: Left-multiplying a layer weight by an orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\) preserves the operator norm of that layer, but could it change the network’s overall Lipschitz constant due to interactions with nonlinearities and residual connections? Have you measured any effect on gradient norms or robustness that could be attributed to orthogonal finetuning?

questions.title: Practical handling of partial blocks when \(d\) is not divisible by \(b\)
questions.question_body: BOFT uses \(2b \times 2b\) orthogonal blocks within each butterfly component. If \(d\) is not a multiple of \(b\), how are the leftover dimensions handled? Do you use smaller blocks, padding, or masks? Does this create non-uniform parameterization across dimensions, and have you observed any adverse effects?

questions.title: Guidance on where to apply BOFT in transformers (Q/K/V, O, MLP, embeddings)
questions.question_body: For large language models and vision transformers, did you find it best to apply BOFT to all linear projections (Q, K, V, O), to MLP layers, and to embeddings? Are there particular submodules where BOFT consistently yields larger gains per parameter? Any ablation results that could guide practitioners under tight budgets?

questions.title: Can BOFT be combined with LoRA additively or multiplicatively?
questions.question_body: Have you experimented with hybrid adapters like \(\mathbf{W}' = \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{W}^0 + \mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\) (multiplicative orthogonal plus additive low-rank), or \(\mathbf{W}' = (\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\)? Do such combinations provide complementary benefits (e.g., BOFT for stability and LoRA for localized updates), or do they introduce optimization conflicts?

questions.title: Interpreting the “weight interpolation” property shown in Figure 1
questions.question_body: The paper mentions an intriguing weight interpolation property due to matrix factorization (referencing a figure). Could you explain mathematically what is being interpolated? For example, does linearly interpolating the Cayley parameters of each butterfly component trace a smooth path in \(SO(d)\)? Is this related to homotopies between \(\mathbf{I}\) and the learned \(\mathbf{R}\), and does it correlate with accuracy vs. interpolation coefficient?

questions.title: Can BOFT’s information-transmission view suggest better-than-butterfly topologies?
questions.question_body: You motivate butterfly via efficient information exchange on grid-structured graphs. Are there alternative sparse topologies (e.g., expander graphs, Bene\v{s} networks, Clos networks) that might yield even better parameter-efficiency or robustness for composing dense orthogonal matrices? Have you tried any of these, and how did they compare to butterfly in practice?
